assessment.nobel_worthiness: A new observational window: the 2013 discovery of a diffuse flux of astrophysical neutrinos at TeV-PeV energies, later tied to the blazar TXS 0506+056 and to the Galactic plane, opened neutrino astronomy. It required instrumenting a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice, which is exactly the instrument-driven discovery I weigh most heavily. The Nobel-level question is the detector concept and the discovery, not any single source identification.
assessment.attribution: Halzen conceived and led the cubic-kilometre IceCube concept and the AMANDA-to-IceCube path; Karle is credited for the detector design, construction and early analysis; Spiering for the AMANDA/IceCube science and the early collaboration. The collaboration is large, and a fair configuration needs a judgement on leadership versus technical founders. The three named people are a defensible set.
assessment.maturity: The diffuse flux has been confirmed in several independent analysis channels (through-going muons, cascades, starting events), and the TXS 0506+056 evidence is independent in time and in multi-messenger follow-up. The sources of the bulk flux are still not understood, but the discovery itself is stable. Timing is good and the instrument has run for over a decade.
uncertainties: Origin of most of the diffuse flux is unresolved, which does not undercut the detection but limits the astrophysical narrative.
Allocation among Halzen, Karle, Spiering and other founders of AMANDA/IceCube is not fully settled; I have not independently verified who made the decisive early design choices.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, from the magic-wavelength proposal to clocks at the 10^-18 level, are a fundamental advance in measurement. They are used for tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy and the prospective redefinition of the second. A very clear invention with large downstream impact, in the spirit of a new measurement technique.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice idea and demonstrated the first Sr lattice clock; Ye drove the precision and systematic-uncertainty frontier with Sr and made the link to frequency combs. The two-person configuration is natural, though Hall and Hansch already recognised combs in 2005 and other lattice-clock groups exist (e.g. in Paris, Boulder NIST, PTB).
assessment.maturity: Several independent groups have reproduced and improved the performance, and the interpretation is stable. Redefinition of the SI second is still pending, which would add a practical seal but is not required for scientific maturity.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2005 prize on frequency combs and with the ion-clock community (Wineland 2012) may make the committee cautious.
Whether other contributors (e.g. in the theory of magic wavelengths or in Yb and Al+ clocks) deserve credit cannot be settled from the supplied list.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The prediction and observation of the quantum spin Hall effect and the identification of Z2 topological insulators created an entire field. The conceptual originality is high, and it was followed by 3D topological insulators, ARPES confirmation and topological materials more broadly. This is outside my own expertise, so I would lean heavily on colleagues in condensed matter.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele supplied the decisive theory (spin-orbit induced QSH state, Z2 invariant); Molenkamp's group made the first experimental observation in HgTe quantum wells following the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal. BHZ and the 3D topological insulator work (Fu, Kane, Mele; Moore, Balents; Hasan; Zhang) leave real attribution issues, since the prize only has three places.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed in many material systems and with independent probes; the field is mature and stable. Recognition is overdue rather than premature.
uncertainties: Credit for the HgTe proposal (Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang) and for 3D topological insulators is not captured by these three names.
I rely on colleagues for the condensed-matter evaluation.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene turned a theoretical flat-band prediction into an experimentally observed correlated insulator and superconductor, and launched moire quantum matter and twistronics. Originality and impact are high, and it is a clean case of a prediction followed by an experimental discovery.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald predicted the flat bands at the magic angle; Jarillo-Herrero's group made the decisive 2018 observations. The experimental discovery of correlated states and superconductivity is clearly his group's work, while earlier theory by Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto is not on the list and may weaken a clean attribution.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced by many groups, but the field is only about eight years old and the nature of the superconductivity and the full phase diagram remain debated. Recognition may be somewhat early, though the core discovery is robust.
uncertainties: Priority questions regarding earlier theory and the role of sample-preparation advances (e.g. hBN encapsulation).
Nature of the superconducting pairing remains unresolved; timing could be considered premature.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED made strong coupling between superconducting qubits and microwave resonators possible, enabling dispersive readout and gates, and is the architecture used by leading quantum processors. The impact is broad, covering both quantum technology and fundamental tests. It is outside my expertise, so I defer to colleagues on the weight given the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits.
assessment.attribution: Blais and colleagues proposed the architecture, Wallraff and Schoelkopf demonstrated strong coupling in 2004; Schoelkopf's group additionally developed the transmon with Yale colleagues, and Devoret and Nakamura are laureates or related to the transmon story. The three names are plausible, though Houck, Koch and others on the transmon are omitted.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced worldwide, with a stable interpretation and a mature technology. The 2025 prize on related superconducting circuits may reduce the chance of immediate recognition, though not the scientific merit.
uncertainties: Proximity to the 2025 prize and overlap with Devoret and Martinis.
Fair attribution relative to the transmon and Yale group contributors is not obvious.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Squeezed-light injection reduces quantum noise in interferometers and is now in routine use in LIGO, Virgo and GEO600, so it improves actual discovery reach. As an instrument builder I value a theoretical idea turned into a deployed, calibrated detector technology.
assessment.attribution: Caves provided the 1981 proposal for squeezed-vacuum interferometry; Kimble made the first experimental squeezed light in 1985 (with Slusher, Wu and others) and later frequency-dependent squeezing; Schnabel developed GEO600-style implementations and the frequency-dependent squeezing proposals. Mavalvala, who is on the longlist for this entry, is a leading experimentalist for LIGO squeezing; I choose three, and others (Slusher, Vahlbruch) arguably have claims.
assessment.maturity: Deployed in operating detectors with demonstrated sensitivity gains, so the technology is verified. The scientific idea is well established, though some may see it as an engineering refinement rather than a new discovery.
uncertainties: The Nobel committee may see this as incremental relative to LIGO's 2017 prize.
Credit among Caves, Kimble, Slusher, Walls, Mavalvala and Schnabel is spread across decades.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Baryon acoustic oscillations are a standard ruler imprinted in the large-scale galaxy distribution, detected in the SDSS and 2dFGRS in 2005. They underpin precision dark-energy and Hubble-tension work and complement supernovae and the CMB.
assessment.attribution: The 2005 detection papers were Eisenstein et al. (SDSS LRG) and Cole et al. (2dFGRS); Peacock is credited here for 2dFGRS leadership. The theoretical origin of the feature (Peebles and Yu; Sunyaev and Zeldovich) is not in the list, and the collaboration nature makes the choice of three people contentious.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed repeatedly by BOSS, eBOSS, 6dF, WiggleZ and DESI, with growing precision; the standard-ruler interpretation is stable. Recent DESI hints of evolving dark energy are still unsettled, so I see no problem for the BAO detection but caution on interpretation.
uncertainties: Theoretical credit for the feature (Peebles and Yu; Sunyaev and Zeldovich) is absent from this list.
Choosing between SDSS and 2dFGRS leaders is a hard allocation of credit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cold-atom quantum simulation of Hubbard models, including the Mott insulator and fermionic Hubbard physics with quantum gas microscopes, gives controllable many-body systems. Impact on many-body physics is large, though it overlaps with the 2001 and 2012 prizes in this area. I defer to colleagues on atomic physics.
assessment.attribution: Greiner demonstrated the bosonic Mott-insulator transition with Hansch and Bloch; Bloch and Esslinger led the optical-lattice and fermionic Hubbard work; Zoller (with Jaksch) proposed the bosonic Hubbard simulator. Zoller's claim is large, and the list gives four names, so I must choose three. I choose the main experimental trio; Zoller is arguably needed, so allocation is unsettled.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced worldwide and now producing quantitative benchmarks, though solving open problems (e.g. the doped Hubbard model's pairing) has not yet been achieved. Timeliness is acceptable but not pressing.
uncertainties: Zoller's theory contribution is substantial and could displace one of the experimentalists.
Whether the simulators have produced a decisive new discovery, as opposed to a capability, is debatable.
